subject: Some simulations on how K values affect estimates of pcountOpen models

messages.author: cf45c6aa992bbacc
messages.subject: Some simulations on how K values affect estimates of pcountOpen models
parts:
Hi all,


I am simulating data sets from a three-level hierarchical model as that described in Hostetler & Chandler(2015) with the pcountOpen argument dynamics="trend".


I have M sites that are visited over T primary periods. In words these are the levels (details in Hostetler & Chandler 2015):

1)  the initial number of individuals available to detection at each site varies according to a Poisson with a certain parameter (lambda).

2) the  number of individuals available to detection after the first primary period at each site depends on a Poisson whose parameter is the product of the number of individuals at the previous primary period times the growth rate (gamma).

3) the number of individuals detected at each site and primary period depends on a Binomial distribution that picks up a certain number of individuals from those available according to a certain parameter (detectability).


I have built the data sets in such a way that all the parameters, lambda, gamma, and detectability, depend linearly each one on a different predictor (distributed uniformly around zero).  Lambda and detectability depends on predictors varying across sites (no over time) and gamma depends on a predictor varying over time (no across sites).

Below some details on the parameter values I have used to simulate the data set. I don't give details on the predictors since I am interested here just on the average of each parameter (i.e. the intercept):


> mean.lambda<- 20 # when back-transformed this will be a Poisson around this value (no. of individuals)

> alpha1<- log(mean.lambda) # on the log scale this is the value of the intercept for lambda

> beta1<- 2 # this is the slope for lambda (on the log scale)

> mean.gamma<- 1 # this is the average growth rate (1= stable population)

> alpha2<- log(mean.gamma)# on the log scale this is the value of the intercept for gamma

> beta2<- 1 # this is the slope for gamma (on the log scale)

> mean.detectability<- 0.05 # this is the average detection probability

> alpha3<- qlogis(mean.detectability) # on the logit scale this is the value of the intercept for the detection probability

> beta3<- 3 # this is the slope for the detection probability (on the logit scale)


This is the summary of the data:

> summary(data$umf)

Then I run a pcountOpen model with the 'true' predictors and want to assess the accuracy of estimates by using the RSS (Residual Sum of Squares) on the back-transformed average estimate of each parameter (lambda, gamma, and detectability): I vary the K values like this:

m200<- pcountOpen(~A1, ~A2, ~1, ~KR, data= data$umf, dynamics= "trend", K= 200)

m300<- pcountOpen(~A1, ~A2, ~1, ~KR, data= data$umf, dynamics= "trend", K= 300)

m400<- pcountOpen(~A1, ~A2, ~1, ~KR, data= data$umf, dynamics= "trend", K= 400)

m500<- pcountOpen(~A1, ~A2, ~1, ~KR, data= data$umf, dynamics= "trend", K= 500)


I have been reading the Dennis et al. (2015) paper which speaks about the effect and choice of K in N-mixture models as well as different posts here in the unmarked forum and I grasped some general ideas: 1) it is known that K may effect HM estimates in some circumstances, 2) sometimes the higher is the K value the higher is the lambda estimate (e.g. see Fig. 2 in the Dennis et al paper), 3) this kind of troubles tend to arise when the detection probability is very low (as in my case, p=0.05).
However here it seems that the larger the K the more accurate the estimates. This seems to be the case for lambda and detectability (gamma is not that sensitive to changes in K). Below is what I get.


Lambda:

> (RSSlambda200<- as.numeric((exp(coef(m200, type="lambda")[1])-mean.lambda)/mean.lambda)^2)

[1] 0.2336284

> (RSSlambda200<- as.numeric((exp(coef(m200, type="lambda")[1])-mean.lambda)/mean.lambda)^2)

[1] 0.2336284

> (RSSlambda300<- as.numeric((exp(coef(m300, type="lambda")[1])-mean.lambda)/mean.lambda)^2)

[1] 0.104415

> (RSSlambda400<- as.numeric((exp(coef(m400, type="lambda")[1])-mean.lambda)/mean.lambda)^2)

[1] 0.02924366

> (RSSlambda500<- as.numeric((exp(coef(m500, type="lambda")[1])-mean.lambda)/mean.lambda)^2)

[1] 0.001135718


Gamma:

> (RSSgamma200<- as.numeric((exp(coef(m200, type="gamma")[1])-mean.gamma)/mean.gamma)^2)

[1] 0.0001515306

> (RSSgamma300<- as.numeric((exp(coef(m300, type="gamma")[1])-mean.gamma)/mean.gamma)^2)

[1] 0.0001392376

> (RSSgamma400<- as.numeric((exp(coef(m400, type="gamma")[1])-mean.gamma)/mean.gamma)^2)

[1] 0.0001278606

> (RSSgamma500<- as.numeric((exp(coef(m500, type="gamma")[1])-mean.gamma)/mean.gamma)^2)

[1] 0.0001159416


Detectability:

> (RSSdetectability200<- as.numeric((plogis(coef(m200, type="det")[1])-mean.detectability)/mean.detectability)^2)

[1] 0.7686299

> (RSSdetectability300<- as.numeric((plogis(coef(m300, type="det")[1])-mean.detectability)/mean.detectability)^2)

[1] 0.1524869

> (RSSdetectability400<- as.numeric((plogis(coef(m400, type="det")[1])-mean.detectability)/mean.detectability)^2)

[1] 0.01365723

> (RSSdetectability500<- as.numeric((plogis(coef(m500, type="det")[1])-mean.detectability)/mean.detectability)^2)

[1] 0.002678777


Have you any practical hint on how one should choose the K value and/or some commentary on this?

Thanks,

 

Simone

Just an (important) update:

I have simulated different data sets (with the same generating parameters I used before) and I have just seen that K=200 was not that bad for accuracy of estimates. However, the same pattern repeats in terms of improved accuracy by increasing K and in terms of better accuracy for gamma than for the other two parameters.
